1. In examining the industrial structure of the Canadian economy, The Standard Industrial Classification published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics has divided activity in Canada into 10 industrial divisions, excluding government departments, broken down into 51 major industry groups. These are further subdivided into industries.
The extent of foreign investment in each of these industries is not readily available at the present time. However, in three industrial divisions, agriculture, forestry and fishing, foreign investment is very small and in another five industrial divisions nonresident owned firms carry on less that 25 per cent of the activity. These industrial divisions are construction, transportation, communication and other utilities, trade, finance and service industries.
In the mining industrial division, oil and gas wells are largely foreign owned while metal and non-metal mines in total are equally divided between resident and non-resident owned companies. Certain of the individual metals are dominated by foreign owned firms while others are dominated by Canadian owned firms.
In the manufacturing industrial division information is available on a basis of 89 industries. In 19 of these industries, more than 75 per cent of the sales are by companies that are more than 50 per cent foreign owned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sought an opportunity to speak in this debate because of a serious and important issue which I wish to discuss. It is my intention to stay with the subject that prompted me to take part in this debate. However, before I get into that question may I say that we in this party regret that the government was not willing to have a debate today on the important question of housing. We are glad that the government is prepared to find a day fairly soon to discuss this matter, but we think a debate ought to have taken place today.
The government may not realize it, but the working press who covered the housing conference and the people of Canada who have read about it, heard it on the radio and seen it on television know it was a colossal failure. The very fact that it wound up in two days instead of the scheduled three days is evidence-

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.

speechtext:
I have only 30 minutes, Mr. Speaker.
December 13, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Knowles

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman says the conference concluded at the end of two days instead of three, has he taken into consideration that it sat on Monday evening and for two extra hours late yesterday afternoon and evening, thus giving the full time that had been anticipated?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The conference was still concluded in two days, and I suggest the reason it did not continue was that the premiers of the various provinces were finding it not worth their while to stay.
Basically the reason the conference failed is that the federal government is not prepared to measure up to its responsibilities in the field of housing. For the federal government to suggest to the conference that its financial contribution to housing in Canada in the next fiscal year is to be $300 million less than it has been this year is hardly the way to make the conference a success. I hope the government will yet realize the importance of this issue and the nature of the role it must play in this important problem.
Hon. members will not be surprised if I indicate that the subject to which I wish to devote most of my remarks this afternoon is the announcement by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) on Thursday, December 7, that it is not the intention of the government to go ahead with the provision of increases in the pensions of retired civil servants. May I say at the outset that when I look over the list of cuts that the President of the Treasury Board announced in his speech last Thursday night, I am impressed with the fact that a good many of them relate to matters that the government did not want to go ahead with anyway. I have a gnawing suspicion that this is the case with respect to increased pensions for retired civil servants.
Let me indicate a few examples which support my contention that many of the cuts simply represent not going ahead with something the government was against doing anyway. For example, it is proposed to cut out the selling of government annuities. No suggestion was made as to how much this is going to save, but it was put forward under the excuse of its being an economy measure. Those of us who have been around here for any length of time know that for many years the insurance companies of this country have been lobbying against the federal government being in the annuity business. The last time the federal government sought to improve the Government Annuities Act was in the year 1951. I remember the occasion very


well. We had a government bill which was given second reading and referred to one of the standing committees of the house. It provided for certain improvements to be made in the Government Annuities Act, but the insurance people came here in force. Although we finally got the bill passed by that standing committe, when it came back to the house the government let it die on the order paper. It is obviously because of its desire to stop pushing the sale of government annuities that the government has dropped the selling of these annuities.
Then I notice that the government has disbanded the special planning secretariat in the Privy Council office. This special planning secretariat was in effect the high command of the war on poverty. How much real interest has the government shown in the war on poverty? This is one area where the government is pacifist, one area where it is prepared not to go to war. It has not shown any real interest in this supposed effort, and so under the excuse of economy the special planning secretariat has been dissolved.
I should like to join with my colleague the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman), in saying a word with respect to the cut that has been handed to the Company of Young Canadians. I know the many criticisms that are made about this organization and the people in it, but the fact of the matter is that these are young people who belong to a generation that maybe some members of this house cannot understand, but they are young people who are concerned about social conditions.
We had a few witnesses before us yesterday in one of the standing committees of the house, including two or three people who had worked with the Company of Young Canadians. I think all of us who were at that committee were impressed with how much knowledge they had of a certain social problem, a knowledge much in advance of that of many of the conventional agencies. Somehow or other the government does not like what the Company of Young Canadians is doing and so, under the excuse of economy, a cut is made in its budget. Incidentally, it is my understanding that the director of the Company of Young Canadians heard only on the television news that a cut was being made in the budget of that organization.
I still do not know where we stand with respect to the Prince Edward Island causeway. One day it is off; another day it is on. I suspect that the government is still uneasy over the fact that it promised it during the
December 13, 1387

last election. The promise did not result in the Liberals winning very many seats in Prince Edward Island and obviously they would like to get out of this project or postpone it. I suggest again, Mr. Speaker, that economy is being used as an excuse when there are really other motives.
I mention just these three or four examples. I could cite others but I do not want to take time away from the subject with which I am mainly concerned today. I merely mention these as situations parallel to the situation with respect to pensions for retired civil servants.
I am convinced that there are voices in the federal cabinet which have never wanted to agree to increased pensions for retired civil servants. I am personally convinced that one of those voices is that of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), and that the so-called drive for economy is now being used simply as an excuse for not going ahead with this proposition which was unanimously recommended on May 8 by a special joint committee of both houses of parliament.
Seldom have a group of people been misled so extensively as have the retired civil servants of the federal government. For many years they have been asked to wait for one thing or another before their plight would be considered. At one time they were told to wait until the Canada Pension Plan was put through.
[DOT] (4:00 p.tn.)
When our Canada Pension Plan committee was in session representatives of the retired civil servants were permitted to appear before that committee to argue their case. They were told, however, that nothing could be done for them under that legislation and that they should wait until it was through. They were told that their situation would be dealt with separately. Also, when old age pensions were being discussed they were told they should wait until that legislation was completed and then their case would be looked into.
A couple of years ago when matters relating to the civil service generally were being discussed they were told that when the coast was clear an opportunity would be made for their whole problem to be discussed by a special joint committee of parliament. That joint committee was given their problem as a term of reference in January, 1967. It held extensive meetings during the early months of this year and made a unanimous report to
The Budget-Mr. Knowles parliament on May 8. It recommended without any qualification that there should be immediate increases in the pensions of retired civil servants.
In our report, when using the phrase "retired civil servants" we made it clear that this should include retired armed forces personnel and retired Royal Canadian Mounted Police personnel as well. Our report also included widows and orphans in all cases. It added up to a comprehensive statement by that committee that this is a problem which parliament should deal with.
Hon. members will remember the atmosphere which prevailed in respect of this matter in May, June and early July. Some of us were on our feet every week in an effort to get the government to act at that time. The type of answers we were given led us to believe that action would be taken before we recessed for the summer. Certain ministers on the other side including the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), cannot deny the assurance they gave me that action would be taken in the month of June. When on July 7 this house was faced with an adjournment some of us opposed that adjournment without action being taken on this question. We lost, but even so we were led to believe then that action would be taken in the fall. We came back on September 25 and the issue has been raised in one way or another by one member or another two or three times a week since then.
We were told repeatedly that the matter was still under consideration, but finally on December 7 the President of the Treasury Board told us a decision had been made not to proceed with these increases. I suggest that this was a cruel way to mislead these people. Their hopes were built up, they were given a feeling of confidence that something would be done, and then they were told that nothing would be done for them either now or during the fiscal year 1968-69. Despite the finality with which the President of the Treasury Board spoke on December 7 and despite the fact that the Prime Minister expressed a hope that this matter could be reconsidered some time which sounded like delaying it for five or ten years, I still appeal to the government to act on this issue during this session of parliament.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to make some specific suggestions concerning what can be done. First, however, may I remind hon.
December 13, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Knowles members on both sides of the house that there are about 36,000 retired civil servants and about 16,000 widows of retired civil servants who are on pension. If you add to these two figures the retired members of the R.C.M.P. and the retired members of the armed forces and then add their widows, you arrive at a total of about 58,000 federal superannuates of various kinds and a total of about 18,000 widows of the various federal superannuates. If hon. members are interested, I might point out that answers to questions of mine have been placed on Hansard of November 22, November 29, December 4 and December 11 which give the numbers of these people living in the various provinces and the number receiving pensions in the various categories. Rather than confuse members with a whole host of statistics may I say that most of these people-I am referring to the retired civil servants rather than the widows-are on pensions of less than $200 a month. The average for the widows is much lower.
There was a time when a $200 pension sounded like something one could live on, but I should like to say to the members of this house that the heart-rending letters I get come not only from people whose pensions are down in the $30, $40 or $50 a month bracket but also from people who have served this country and this government for many years and who retired a few years ago on a pension of $150 to $175 a month. These people have seen living costs rise so many times in the decade since they retired that they are now living in virtual poverty.
I submit that the federal government of this country as an employer has a responsibility to these people. What can it do to discharge that responsibility? Let me say that you will never convince these people, no matter how many arguments you advance on the basis of figures, that they are not entitled to increases in pension on the basis of the money they paid in and which is in the superannuation fund. When you tell them that the money is not there, that it is only so many figures on a book and that these figures are there to protect future retirees you do not solve the problem for them.
These people know that on the books of the superannuation fund at the present time there is an amount approaching $3 billion. They know also that the interest paid on that fund each year is greater than the amount that is paid out each year in pensions. They know the fund is growing by leaps

and bounds. They do not understand why they cannot be paid out of that fund. Roughly speaking, what is happening at the present time is that each fiscal year about $100 million is being paid into the fund by employees who are working and paying their percentage. About $100 million is put in by the government to match the employees' contributions. Something approaching $100 million is put in by the government as interest on the fund that is there. I say "put in"; the employees put the money in because they do not get it in their pay cheques, but apparently it gets used right away. So there is a total of about $300 million a year credited to the superannuation account while the amount being paid out in pensions to the people who are now retired is only $75 million to $80 million a year.
How can any member of this house explain to these people that they cannot have their money in the form of a pension because there must be some kind of an economy drive? I do not accept the reasons for the cut or the budget or the economic plans this government has, but even if these plans are to be gone ahead with by this government one cannot explain to these people why, since the money is there, they should not receive increased pensions. If the members of the government feel that they must not touch the money now being credited-that is what they say-because it is put there for future retirees or, on the other hand, if they say that the money really is not there, what confidence does that give present employees for their time of retirement
Let me remind the government of what I thought was a very useful suggestion made by the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada last session relating to the rate of interest the government pays on this money. The rate of interest which this government pays-mind you, it is only so many figures in a book-is 4 per cent. That is a pretty cheap rate of interest to pay on money today. The suggestion has been made that the government might consider paying 5 per cent on that money. I wonder whether hon. members realize that if that were done, if an additional one per cent were paid on the money in the fund, this would produce an extra $25 million or $30 million a year. That would be sufficient to increase the pension of every retired civil servant, every widow of a retired civil servant, and the others I have mentioned, the armed forces and R.C.M.P. personnel, by about one third of their present
December 13, 1967	COMMONS
pension. To put it round figures, this would mean an average pension increase to every superannuate of about $60 to $65 per month. Hon. members can do this figuring for themselves if they read the figures which appear in the various issues of Hansard to which I have referred, and if they will look at the figures in the estimates and elsewhere.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
All the government has to do today is admit that interest rates have gone up everywhere. Interest rates on housing and bank loans have gone up to 8 per cent or more. This government should be fair and credit these people with 5 per cent interest on their own money in the fund which would provide a sufficient amount to make it possible for the government to increase the pensions of all our retired civil servants, members of the armed forces, members of the R.C.M.P and their widows by an average of one-third of the pensions they now receive. In dollars and cents terms this would amount to $60 or $65 per month for every pensioner. I am not suggesting that it should be a flat one third across the board increase because I am aware of the fact that certain adjustments should be made, but I give this figure to indicate what would be possible if the government followed the suggestion made by the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, supported by the Public Service Alliance of Canada, to our committee.
There is no use in the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) trying to tell these people that this is a matter involving a cash position versus figures on the books, and so on. These people had money deducted from their pay cheques which they did not get. The same is true of civil servants working today. A deduction of 5 per cent or 6J per cent is being made from their pay cheques. They do not get that money. Where does it go? Does it go into a fund out of which pensions are paid? No, this money becomes figures in the books. The government is spending this money and it should pay interest on it.
These civil servants are assured that the reason they will receive pensions when they retire is that the government is there behind them. If they have to count on the government being behind them 10, 20 or 30 years from now the way the government is behind retired civil servants today in respect of their pensions this will not make for a very happy situation. That is no doubt the reason that Mr. Trevor Gough of the Public Service
DEBATES	5385
The Budget-Mr. Knowles Alliance of Canada wrote such a strong letter to the Prime Minister a day or two after the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) announced the decision of the government not to go ahead with this matter.
There is no question in my mind that there is a need. These people clearly have a right to an increase, and even though the President of the Treasury Board stood up in this house and said the government did not commit itself in black and white that it would raise pensions by a certain date, it did commit itself that it would deal with this matter on the basis of the report to parliament by the special joint committee of both houses.
We hear a great deal these days about what could be done to improve parliament by strengthening the committee system. If this is an example of how the government is going to strengthen committees it should not bother. The committee to which I referred was chaired by Senator Bourget and the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard). This committee held hearings for a considerable period of time over more than a year. It dealt with many matters involving the civil service. It went into these things exhaustively. The committee was made up of members of all parties in both houses and represented all points of view, social, economic and otherwise; yet it came up with a unanimous recommendation that these pensions should be increased. For the government not to follow this recommendation is an insult to the committee and to the committee system, and certainly it is an offence to those people who are affected by this whole situation.
I see that my time is running out and I will have to say in a very few minutes what I wanted to say to put this special problem in the context of a larger problem that is very much with us and will be with us in increasing terms as time passes. People sometimes ask me about other pensioners and whether they should not also receive an increase in their pensions. The answer is a resounding yes. That goes for railway workers and all our pensioners. The day has to come and come soon when the principle is recognized that people who retire should not be compelled to live for the rest of their lives on a fixed pension.
Let me put it this way. There are people retiring in 1967 at younger ages, at 60 and so on, who no doubt have a chance of being alive in the year 2000. Some ten years from now there will be many people retiring who
December 13, 1967

The Budget-Mr. Knowles will have a good chance of living until the year 2000. Does anyone in this place imagine that people in the year 2000, will be able to live under the conditions we will have then on pensions fixed in the years 1967, 1970 or 1975? We must reach the point where there is built into any pension scheme arrangements for pensions to escalate as time passes. This situation is true for all other sections of society. No one expects workers, farmers, businessmen or people in ordinary jobs to spend all their working lives, from the time they are 21 until they are 65, on a fixed income. It is the nature of things for costs to go up and living standards to improve. People are entitled to meet these higher costs and share in these higher standards of living. Where is there any common sense in the suggestion that when you reach 60 or 65 years of age and retire this process must stop? Pensions have to be subject to escalation.
The government can tell us it recognizes this principle, and it has in respect of old age security and the Canada Pension Plan, but this has been a very meagre recognition. Everybody knows what will happen in respect of old age security in January. It is to increase by $1.50. That is a recognition, but it is pretty meagre. It is not good enough to do just that. I suggest we must do this across the board and on a scale to keep up with rising costs and rising standards of living.
I am satisfied in my own mind that the reason the governmment does not want to grant this increase in pensions to its own employees is that it is afraid business will then say it has been put on the spot and must do the same thing. That is the trouble with this government. It never leads and never faces up to problems which require leadership.
It is not good enough to wait until 1980, 1990 or 2000 to discover that our whole pensions structure has fallen apart because we did not make provision for pensions to escalate. The time for leadership in this regard is now, and I suggest the place for the government to begin is in respect of its own employees. That is why I take as strong a stand as I do in support of retired civil servants and other retired employees of the federal government, of the Canadian National Railways, and so on. They have a right of their own and they have their own needs. The government has an obligation to them as an employer and also because of the need to establish a principle that must be carried through the whole of our economy.

Let me return to the position I took at the beginning of my remarks. The government has committed a cruel hoax on these people by giving them the hope that something was going to be done. It is time for the government to undo the harm and offence it has done to these people. It is time to stop the policy of discouraging them. The government must act in respect of this question.
There are broad policies that can be worked out in the next few years with regard to pension increases across the board and they must be worked out. But there is no excuse whatsoever for the announcement of last Thursday night contained in paragraph 13 of the list of cut-backs by the President of the Treasury Board. This money is available and I call upon the government to implement the recommendation of the special joint committee on the public service of Canada during this session. I call upon the government to increase the pensions of our retired civil servants, former members of the armed forces and the R.C.M.P., their widows and all our federal superannuates. The time for this action, Mr. Speaker, is now.

The Budget-Mr. Otto
itself into a financial morass because of political pressures. The fact is that the government at all times has tried to resist the political pressures that have been applied by hon. gentlemen opposite. Time after time we have had votes of confidence because hon. gentlemen opposite wanted more money to be spent and the government was forced into the position of resisting increases in spending. So that is not the issue.
The issue comes about to a great extent because of the report of the Carter commission. I agree wholeheartedly with the minister when he says that the Carter report cannot be adopted in toto. I also believe the minister when he says that the government will introduce very serious reforms in respect of fiscal policy. I believe they are needed. I shall try to explain my position with regard to the Carter report and why I think it cannot be adopted.
The Carter report is, of course, a very fine document. Surprisingly, the commission was chaired by a member of the establishment who will probably lose his membership in the National Club, the York Club, and so on, because of the report. Although vast changes are envisaged in the report and it contains many suggested reforms, in one way it is just as hidebound, just as restrictive, as our present fiscal policies.
For example, it is said of the Carter report that when faced with hard choices between equity and economic expansion the commissioners consistently gave the greatest weight to the objective of equity. This means they are taking the very ancient viewpoint of taxation, namely, that taxation is merely a burden to be shared, in other words, that we should share the poverty. The modern concept of taxation is not merely to share the burdens of the cost of government but it also has a great deal to do with our economic destiny, industrial expansion, area industrialization, balance of trade and efficiency of production. All these things have a great bearing on the question and are indeed controlled by the tax incentives given to industry.
The most important part of taxation today is that which affects industrial expansion, employment, or what we might call the destiny of industrial expansion. Second is equity. If equity is the first principle, as the Carter commission said, it cannot apply today because if this were the case the whole ARDA program would be out, the whole industrial incentive program would be out.

December 13, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Otto
Obviously it is not fair to give a farmer in one area a tax advantage and not give it to another, as the Carter commission report suggests in respect of horizontal equity.
The commission says that the prime objective of taxation policy is equity, but that cannot apply today. Therefore it cannot apply as far as the government is concerned. There is another principle that we must examine very carefully. The commission would tax the command of goods and services and not the consumption of goods and services. But I wonder whether it is desirable today to tax the command or control of goods and services. If those goods and services are used for industrial expansion, would we not be penalizing those who have this command at the expense of industrial expansion?
I believe we should at all times tax the consumption of goods and services, and possibly the command of goods and services where that command is not of benefit to the nation. But where the command of goods and services is beneficial to the country through providing additional employment and industrial growth, to impose a tax strictly because of a very hidebound principle such as the Carter report seems to contain is wrong, and this principle cannot be applied today.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I have no particular quarrel, and I think very few businessmen in Canada have, with a tax on capital gains and a tax on inheritances. But all these things must be pliable. I believe this is the essence of what the minister is trying to get at when he says that reforms will be made. If they are made, I believe we have to be very flexible in these areas. A capital gains tax on land-I shall refer to this matter later-would be beneficial today. But to impose a capital gains tax on the return of risk capital may not be the thing to do. What we need today is a flexible policy whereby a capital gains tax need not be imposed on all capital gains. Indeed, the same applies to inheritance and corporation taxes.
I heartily endorse the recommendation of the Carter commission that corporations should be taxed once, whether the money is in the hands of the corporations or in the hands of the shareholders. But I think we all agree that this must not be an inflexible rule because in some cases it would be advantageous to tax the profits of the corporation and not those of the shareholders and in other cases the reverse would apply. In other words, if the corporation reinvests its money

and expands its industrial potential it is obviously of advantage to the nation not to tax the corporation but rather the shareholders. On the other hand, if this principle is applied inflexibly, as is suggested by the Carter commission, we will find that people will demand shares in companies which always pay good dividends, regardless of their reserve for expansion and growth. So what we want is flexibility.
I agree with the views of the Carter com-mission'with regard to expense accounts, not necessarily because their recommmendation is fair but because I believe that expense accounts do not make good, efficient producers. High living at the expense of corporations must not continue if we expect employees in the lower echelons and workmen to work efficiently. An esprit de corps must exist in industry because it increases efficiency. For this reason I am definitely opposed to expense account living. I believe that it ruins efficient production and therefore I agree with the recommendation of the Carter commission with regard to this subject.
Now I should like to say a word or two with regard to the demand for homes, land development, etc. There is no necessity to repeat that there is a housing crisis in Canada today, because we all know it. It has also been said that there is no money to deal with this problem properly. I suggest we do not need money. The first thing we need is the guts to make changes. Of course, money is required to some extent, but what we really need now is a decision to change the circumstances which make houses very expensive.
Let me put it this way. I can safely say to anyone, and I can back it up with figures, that construction costs today are less than they were 15 years ago when one considers what one gets in material, handling, premanufacture, etc. The construction industry has been very efficient and has kept up to date. This leaves one cause for the crisis in homes-land. The price of land has increased enormously. In 1951 I paid $1,200 for a lot. Now I am paying $16,000 for a smaller lot in the city of Toronto. Historically the price of land has always gone up because it is a hedge against inflation. There is no sense in buying diamonds if you want to ensure that the value of your money will remain the same. What you should do is buy land, and there is tremendous pressure exercised by people who want to buy land strictly as a
December 13, 1967

hedge against inflation. This applies to insurance companies, pension plans, and all people who wish to ensure that 15 or 20 years from now their money will have the same value in proportion to the price of goods. This is a historical fact.
How must we combat this problem? First of all, we must recognize its existence. At this point may I suggest-and I hope the Minister of Finance is listening-that some form of accelerated bonds might be put on the market, the value of which would rise with the cost of living. This would be another hedge against inflation and would remove the pressure on land. I know this is a radical suggestion but it is now being considered by a well known United States insurance company which is studying the possibility of paying insurance benefits in real money because it recognizes the tremendous pressure on land.
One cannot make more land, but the demand for it increases steadily. As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) said, cities can be further expanded by the addition of suburbs which would have to be made accessible to and from the centre in no more than 20 to 23 minutes or half an hour at the most. A new form of transportation must be introduced, namely, rapid transit systems. This will make suburbs attractive.
There is another point which could be considered by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue. People who own land are granted all sorts of exemptions from income tax. We give them exemptions for real estate taxes. Land owners and speculators receive all kinds of advantages. No one but speculators would take issue with the minister if he were to say he is going to impose a capital gains tax on land speculators or on anyone who sells land because, as everyone knows, these people cannot lose money on their transactions. Since no risk is involved, why are these people given an exemption in respect of capital gains?
The municipalities in turn foster higher land prices by allowing land to remain stagnant and by giving tax concessions on vacant land. Indeed, back in the 1940's the city of Winnipeg applied a very good principle whereby land purchased from the city was allowed to be taxed as vacant land in the first year and thereafter was taxed as if a building were on it. As a result there was no land speculation because it was not worth while. In 1946 I bought land in Winnipeg for $1.65 per foot of frontage. Today it is worth $3 or $4, and it is in the suburbs.

I think the Habitat scheme should be modified to allow people to own their homes. Obviously they would not want to live in the middle of a cube structure. This will have to be modified. N.H.A. mortgage insurance for homes should be reduced from $18,000 to $12,000.

Essentially this is a provincial matter and only partially under the jurisdiction of the federal government. We must have the guts to say: We will take over the area, zone it and build on it or have someone build on it; if the township or municipality will not take it over, we will make it our own municipality. Essentially municipal politicians are agents of the established people. It is the home owners who elect the municipal politicians to represent them. These politicians do not care about people without homes. They are our headache. We will never get the municipalities to speed up the pace of development. Someone else must do it. I suggest that the province could establish a principle in this regard to the effect that as long as a subdivider or land developer abides by these regulations there will be no trouble. I had to go to 37 meetings before I could get a piece of land subdivided. This involved a lapse of time of about four and a half years. There is no hope that the waiting period will be reduced because these people resist changes of that sort.
With regard to finding more money, I suggest to the minister that a great deal of money that could be used for N.H.A. financing is now being used for short-term investment. This money goes into the banks for 90 or 180 days and billions of dollars are used by the finance companies in this way. By breaking down national housing mortgages into small units this money could be lent for short-term investment purposes and as a result over a long-term period we could derive about $2.5 billion.
Another point is this, Mr. Speaker. In my own case, if my creditors, especially my suppliers and labourers, could be assured that having built my house they would still get their money I am sure many of them would provide credit for the building of homes. I suggest that C.M.H.C. should insure not only mortgages but also creditors to an amount equal to the value of the home. For example, tradesmen and suppliers could be given a certificate for the equivalent amount of the work or materials supplied which

December 13, 1967
Ways and Means
would guarantee payment. When the home was	sold these certificates would be
redeemed. The creditors would all be paid, and I would suggest that as a result more houses would be built.
There is a shortage of money, of course, and people are becoming less and less inclined to lend money for mortgage purposes. They would rather buy equity stocks. Conventional sources of mortgage money will be more and more hesitant to lend. Changes are required, but we must have the guts to make them.
A word about the Carter report in conclusion, Mr. Speaker. The Carter report is a very inflexible document. I believe that the minister is going to introduce reforms which will give it flexibility and will impose a capital gains tax in some instances and not in others. In this way fiscal policy can be brought to bear on industrial expansion rather than merely equity investments.

It was stated in the spring budget speech of 1966 that it was not intended that the taxation of these goods should remain as a permanent feature of the federal tax structure. It is said that increased demand for tobacco results from our increased population. In this day and age it seems that the younger you are, the harder you smoke. After the war, as many of us remember, a heavy special tax was imposed on cigarettes and tobacco in Canada. AID PROGRAM-SUGGESTED INCLUSION OF FAMILY PLANNING ASSISTANCE TO DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to including in its external aid program, family planning assistance U>
developing countries requesting such assistance, and that the government of Canada should take a more active role at the United Nations and its specialized agencies in supporting measures dealing with world population problems.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is tempting in considering the whole subject of external aid in a debate of this type to begin by discussing whether or not we are doing enough. A recommendation was made a few years ago at the first United Nations conference on trade and development that the developed countries should give 1 per cent of their gross national product toward external aid. We have not reached that target yet. However, time is limited and I shall attempt to keep to the subject of the motion.
Many of us are not satisfied with the total effort Canada is making in the field of external aid. However, it can still be said that this country is doing a great deal. We give food to countries which need it, capital in the form of money and equipment, and we are sending skilled manpower to help operate installations built in the developing countries. In addition we have given a considerable amount of aid to education. The government has done a good deal in this direction and there are many private agencies which have a good record in the field of external aid.
However, there seems to be one blind spot m relation to the question of population which is one of the most important problems facing the developing countries. A year ago a declaration on population was drawn up and presented to heads of government through the United Nations. This declaration was returned to the Secretary General of the United Nations two days ago in New York I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) whether he had been invited to sign it because I noted he had not done so.
I should like to make it clear that I am not one of those who oversimplify this problem. I am not one of those who say that if the developing countries would only do something about birth control and family planning all their problems would be solved. I realize it is not as simple as that. Many things have to be done if we are to minimize
5394	COMMONS
Suggested External Aid Program the suffering from famine which I think will surely come in the years ahead. We need to increase the production of food in this country for export to places where it is needed. We must help the developing countries to increase their own production and to develop both primary and secondary industries. And we must maintain our aid to education. I am, however, suggesting that the question of population is a most important one and that it should be considered by the Canadian government in its external aid program.
Many experts have predicted that whatever is done there will be very serious famine in the world within the next ten years. In recent years there has been famine in India particularly, but from now on famine is likely too occur in many parts of the world in spite of the best efforts we make. I am suggesting we could do certain things to reduce the effect of the famine which hundreds of millions will be facing.
I should like to quote briefly from a speech made on November 24, 1966 by Mr. Herbert H. Lank, chairman of the board of Dupont of Canada Limited, in an address to members of the Society of Chemical Industry, which has since been reprinted in a booklet called "Production And Reproduction, The Great Imbalance." Speaking of the famine threatening the world, Mr. Lank had this to say;

December 13, 1967
earlier, there were one billion people living in the' world. It had taken all of the time before that to reach that figure.
There are various estimates as to what the population of the world will be at the end of this century. A few conservative estimates put it at something less than six billion, or about double the present population, and there are other estimates which put the figure much higher at somewhere around seven billion.
I have just been reading the minutes of the external relations committee of the Senate, volume No. 1, for Thursday, December 7. Mr. Maurice Strong, director of external aid, was the witness, and in reply to a question about the population of the world he said:
Bv the year 2000 the population could rise to more than seven billion; even with a 30 per cent decrease in fertility the figure would be six billion.
The chairman then asked him what is the present population and he replied:
About 3.3 billion, which would be a little less than doubled at the six billion figure.
But, in terms of food production, this means that even to maintain the present inadequate nutritional levels in the less developed world, we will have to double the world's present food production by the end of the century. This involves matching in the next 33 years everything we have been able to achieve in food production since the beginning
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Famine will probably reach serious proportions in India, Pakistan and mainland China in the next three years. Indonesia, Iran, Turkey, Egypt, Brazil and a number of other countries are only a few years behind this timetable. Tens of thousands of children who will die of starvation within the next decade have not yet been conceived.
Complete anarchy could occur if hunger gets the upper hand in three-quarters of the world. We can hardly expect to escape the repercussions of such a catastrophe.
Storm signals are already flying. There were food riots in India again this year. In some parts of Africa there have been six consecutive years of drought. Fortunately, Australian production of cereals and animal foodstuffs will be better this year than last. But drought and flood in China will reduce this year's grain crops to the lowest in five years.
He was speaking of last year. Whenever we get into this subject I think it is necessary to quote figures which show the population growth in the world. I know hon. members may have heard them before but the figures are quite staggering and illustrate the extent of the problem. Today there are three billion plus people living in the world. In 1900, at the beginning of this century, there were two billion people. In 1800, 100 years
Even if many countries of the world adopt methods to try to control the size of families, the population of the world will approximately double by the end of the century, and that really is not a very long time away. However, the earth will not be any bigger. It will still be the same size as it was when we went to school and learned the facts and figures about the size of the earth, how many square miles of land it contains, how many square miles of ocean, and how much of the land is productive. The earth may become more productive. We may get more yield per acre in many parts of the world, but I suggest it will not be that much more productive. In fact in recent years the increase in population has been 2 per cent a year for the world as a whole and the increase in food production has been about 1 per cent a year. We cannot win at that rate.
When famine comes, and it is almost a certainty in the next 10 to 20 years in different parts of the world, we in Canada probably will not suffer. We will have enough to eat but other people will not. It is altogether unlikely that the food supply can be
[Mr. Prittie.l
December 13, 1967

increased rapidly enough to feed the increased population.
I have heard of various schemes to produce food from the ocean. I have heard of various plans to produce wonder foods on land, to produce synthetic food from chemicals. These things may happen some time but we should not count on them. We must count on the fact that food production in the world will continue to increase at a much slower rate than the people of the world will continue to increase.
There are many factors which block rapid increase in food production. Some of them are historical and cultural. It is hard to get people in underdeveloped lands to change their ways. It requires a long educational process to achieve that. It is possible that there will be more intensive use of fertilizers and the building of more plants to make fertilizers, but I suggest these things will not happen in time to prevent a very great shortage of food in the years ahead.
We can count on the fact that for the remainder of the twentieth century the production of people will greatly outstrip the production of food. Some countries have recognized the problem of the very great increase in world population and have realized that something must be done about it. Some of the developing countries have recognized the problem but others have not. For various religious and cultural reasons some countries will not face up to the problem, but others are ready to accept the idea that something should be done. India and Pakistan are two countries where there are no religious barriers to family planning.
Some of the developed countries which supply aid to underdeveloped countries have taken steps to meet the problem. The United States is one of them. This is something which I have followed with a great deal of interest. I first became aware of the subject when I was a parliamentary observer at the United Nations in 1962. At that time one of the committees I was attending, the second committee, was debating this subject. That year, for the first time, the United States government changed its position. Prior to that time, whenever there was a vote on population matters the United States had taken the same position as Canada had and which I believe Canada still takes. They both abstained. But that year, on orders from President Kennedy, the United States delegation cast a vote in favour of a resolution which called for the United Nations to take

I suggest that it earmark certain funds to be made available to countries which wish aid in family planning. If the government is not willing to do this directly I suggest that it consider giving some money to agencies which are willing to do so.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out the importance of this problem in very real terms. Let us take a country like India where there are hundreds and thousands of starving people. I am sure all of us have seen pictures of cities such as Bombay and Calcutta which show wretched-looking people lying on the street with their ribs prominently exposed and also beggars in the street. These people do not have enough to eat. If Indian families can be persuaded to have two children instead of three, or five children instead of six or seven, then the problem could be alleviated to that extent. India and Pakistan are quite willing to accept this kind of aid from Canada, from the United States, from the United Nations or from any source which is willing to give such help.
Finally I should like to say that I do not wish to oversimplify the question of external aid. This is just one aspect of it. Increased food production by the farmers of Canada is very important. Increased food production by the people of the developing countries is very important. But let us not ignore this very important aspect of the whole problem of world population and how to feed people. Feeding the people is not the only problem faced by these countries. They do have to find food, but a rapidly increasing population means that somehow or other they also have to find schools, housing and all the public facilities which are necessary. They simply cannot cope with the problem they have today. They deserve some help from us in this particular field.

subtopic: AID PROGRAM-SUGGESTED INCLUSION OF FAMILY PLANNING ASSISTANCE TO DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to
IMr. Prittie.l
respond to the hon. member under three particular headings. First I should like to deal with the philosophical background of the problem of carrying out a particular policy in which there may be a contest among the principal religious groups in this country. Second, I should like to place on the record, for the benefit of the hon. member and the house generally, the actual approach which Canada has taken in international discussions. From this it will be seen that his generalities perhaps are a little out of date. Third, I should like to make some mention of the recent international discussions which have taken place in this field and make more particular reference to the international programs which are currently in existence with regard to population control.
First, therefore, the philosophical aspect of the problem, which the hon. member has acknowledged, is not removed from the controversy which has taken place principally among people of different religious convictions in this country concerning the propriety or otherwise of section 150(2)(c) of the Criminal Code. As a Protestant and a long-standing advocate of the amendment of this section I certainly would have no personal difficulty in seeing the government of Canada respond to a request for technical assistance and aid in dealing with the major international problem of population control. But as an elected representative, and one having some association with the government, I should like to suggest that not only this government but any Canadian government would have to take into account the difference of opinion which at the moment at least exists between the two principal religious groups in this country. I recognize the responsibility of taking into account the religious convictions of a very substantial minority of Canadians, a very large number of Canadians, whose religious views differ from mine.
In the face of our internal Canadian policy on this question, I believe the arguments for altering our law within Canada are unanswerable and I am glad the government has taken the initiative by introducing a bill in the Senate. As the hon. member knows, most of the Protestant churches are in favour of family planning not only in a permissive manner but in certain circumstances in an imperative manner. It is therefore contrary to the fundamental concept of our society that conduct which a very large religious group regards as proper should be declared
December 13, 1967

to be criminal. Those who do not share that religious belief are not under any imperative to practice family planning. But for those who do believe in family planning there should be that freedom of choice without running into jeopardy in the face of the criminal law.
I think it is only fair, however, to relate the argument put forward by persons of other religious faith that in dealing with foreign policy on this question the exact reverse of the logic applies with regard to Canadian participation in international aid projects. With regard to the amendment to the Criminal Code to abolish section 150(2)(c), those of us who are abolitionists could quite legitimately say that it should be a matter of our personal choice as to what we do and that that choice in no way binds others. The argument which has been turned on us by those who oppose family planning assistance in the international context is that their funds, taken from them by the general tax system, are being used to further practices which, on religious grounds, they abhor. They say that the freedom of action which I claim for myself would not be reciprocated if they must, like it or not, see their taxes go for family planning at the international level. The logic of that argument compels recognition even though I do not share the premise upon which it is founded.
I am cognizant of the very intensive consideration which this question of family planning, and particularly the question of the world population explosion, is now receiving within the highest councils of the Roman Catholic Church. I am cognizant of the fact that many leaders of that church both in Canada and abroad have expressed support for a change in the church's doctrine. I am hopeful that an effective accommodation between that doctrine and the awesome reality of the world population explosion can be achieved. I also hope for a definitive conclusion in the near future of the re-examination of traditional Catholic doctrine on this question. I think the hon. member would be the first to agree that it is better to make a change by persuasion, particularly a change on the basis of religious faith, rather than attempt to do it irrespective of belief.
Principles which have governed the government of Canada in the field of external aid with regard to family planning are several. I should like to take the opportunity to set them out for the benefit of the house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AID PROGRAM-SUGGESTED INCLUSION OF FAMILY PLANNING ASSISTANCE TO DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
speechtext:
1 think it is an
indisputable fact that the question of economic development alone cannot be solved without some resolution of the world population problem. It is because of the very awesome nature of this problem that the policies I am about to set out have been followed by the government. As I have said, surely any government of this country should take into account the religious convictions, which at the moment happen to be opposed, of two very large religious groups and should arrive at a policy which we would hope at least would offend neither.
* (5:30 p.m.)
The first principle that should apply in this field is that the initiative for action should come from the governments of the developing countries. Indeed, one could say in general terms that this is the thrust of all international aid programs. The initiative and requests for aid should come from developing countries, particularly where population pressures present the gravest problems for the economic development and well-being of their societies. It is quite reasonable for developed countries, the United Nations organizations and others, to look for a decision by the developing countries in respect of a request for this kind of assistance, and then carry out aid programs in co-operation with the countries in order to deal with population problems.
The second foundation of our Canadian view on this matter is that the United Nations, particularly through agencies included under its own budget such as the United Nations development program and UNICEF, and specialized agencies such as UNESCO, FAO and the world health organization, are particularly well placed to respond in an effective manner to requests for information and other assistance on the question of population problems from developing
5398	COMMONS
Suggested External Aid Program countries. It is in this respect that we have been prepared to support the United Nations' endeavours in this regard.
In respect of our bilateral program I should like to say that the bilateral program, contrary to what the hon. member for Bur-naby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) suggested, is not one in respect of which Canada has received a request from any developing country for assistance. This is the practice followed in this field throughout the world. Canada has not received any requests for bilateral assistance from any developing country. The hon. member mentioned India and Pakistan. No such request has been forthcoming. It has been the view of Canadian authorities that we would be in a position to respond to requests for help in certain specialized fields which are central to the problem of population control, such as demographic and sociological studies.
I should like to refer in this regard to the report of the fourteenth session of the population commission which is United Nations document W/CN.9/219 published in October, 1967. It gives the results of a study and a description of the problems of family planning, and at page 9, paragraph 17, the following is stated:
The growing importance of population trends as a factor in development calls for a more systematic and detailed study of ail factors influencing population growth, its structural changes and the consequences arising therefrom. Nuclei of staff with demographic and related types of background and training are only just beginning to emerge in the developing countries, however; the lack of professional staff in these fields is being increasingly felt. Requirements for professionally trained persons grow constantly, whereas training itself is a slow process.
It is this kind of thing to which the government of Canada is prepared to respond. The report continues at page 11 to emphasize the importance of demographic studies in an approach to this particular problem. In respect of bilateral assistance I think it is fair to note that except for Sweden no bilateral assistance was forthcoming in this field until approximately 1964 or 1965. Since that time three Scandinavian countries, the United States and the United Kingdom have been providing assistance.
The hon. member referred to his experience at the United Nations during the 1962 general assembly. I do not argue with the position that he took, but I should like to point out that the position of the government of Canada in respect of this international council has changed. More particularly it was

DEBATES	December 13, 1967
changed during the 1965 summer meeting of the economic and social council of the United Nations. That was the first year that Canada was represented on that council in its current term. This is a three-year term and it expires at the end of this month.
The question of population control was brought before the economic and social council as a result of the delivery of the report of the thirteenth session of the population commission which has made an extensive study of the problem. At that time the economic and social council adopted, with the positive support of Canada-not just an abstention but an active vote-a resolution with regard to assistance by the United Nations and its specialized agencies to help resolve this problem in respect of population control. This is economic and social council resolution 1084 dated July 30, 1965.
Let me refer to some of the provisions of this resolution to indicate the endorsement given by the economic and social council to these endeavours by United Nations agencies with the positive support of Canada. The resolution endorsed the recommendation in a resolution of the thirteenth session on the long range program of work in the fields of population, including its recommendation with regard to the increase and improvement of demographic statistics, the strengthening of regional demographic training and research centres, and other activities to increase the supply of technically trained personnel in the developing countries, expansion and intensification of research and technical work, widening of the scope and increase of the amount of technical assistance in population fields.
The resolution also called to the attention of the general assembly the need to provide, within the framework of decisions taken to balance the budgets of the United Nations, funds for the United Nations to carry out the intensified and expanded program of activities in the fields of population, recommended by the population commission. It also recommended consultation with other specialized agencies of the United Nations as to the co-ordinated program which might be followed in the population field. One of the particular impacts of that resolution was the authorization of further action by the United Nations development program, a program to which Canada in recent years has provided financial support. It has provided over $10
December 13, 1967

million this year. This is a program undertaken by the U.N.D.P. to assist those countries which request assistance in respect of population control.
The resolution of the economic and social council, which was passed with Canadian support, was further supported by a resolution passed by the twenty first general assembly and the second committee, on which I had the honour to be representing the government of Canada. This is dated December 29, 1966 and is general assembly resolution 2211. I think several aspects of that resolution are of value because they indicate the approach the United Nations has taken to this question of international assistance to family planning.
The general assembly resolution recognized the need for further study of the growth structure and demographic distribution of population to economic and social development, including national health, nutrition, technical and social welfare programs to be carried out at all levels of government activity. It also recognized the sovereignty of nations in formulating their own population policies with due regard to the principle that the size of a family should be according to the free choice of each individual family. The members of the house will note that this also recognizes the sovereignty of individual countries to make their own decisions. The resolution also notes with satisfaction the success of efforts by the world health organization, the economic and social council and other United Nations entities in promoting assistance in family planning.
I think I can say with some justice to the hon. member and to the house that the position of 1962 has been reversed and that in respect of international multilateral institutions the government of Canada has been prepared to support resolutions in favour of family planning and population control and is prepared to continue to provide funds to these institutions in order that they may carry out their functions, including these programs.

Initiatives which have been taken by the U.N.D.P. have also been matched in the World Health Organization to which Canada is a contributor and has given its support, in the Food and Agricultural Organization to which Canada is also a contributor, and in

I would not like to mention UNICEF without referring to the leadership given to that organization by the deputy minister of National Health and Welfare, Dr. Joseph Willard, who has been chairman of the executive committee of UNICEF for the past two years, and particularly to our late colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg South, Mrs. Margaret Konantz, who played such an active part in the role of UNICEF in this country.
Canadians have been active in the international institutions in dealing with this important problem of population control. The Canadian government, by its formal votes both in ECOSOC and in the general assembly, has given support to the proposals put forward and has seen that funds made available to these multilateral agencies have been applied in carrying out these United Nations resolutions.
In the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I think it can legitimately be said that it has been a useful occupation of the hon. member to bring this important question before the house. I think he would agree that his rather pessimistic assessment of the role of the government of Canada in this field has not been justified and we have been active in the international field in supporting these measures.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you for your remarks, but now I would like to point out in turn that, if we are to help foreign countries, we must first try to find the money. This is exactly what I am doing. Money is needed to accomplish something, for nothing can be done without it.
So, Mr. Speaker, we are convinced that our present system is an impediment to peace and disarmament; it gives rise to commercial abuses which degenerate into international conflicts. That is the cause of the serious problems we are experiencing at this time. What other countries are requesting is the means for self-financing, so they can meet their needs for adequate living conditions.
The financial pump is primed for tremendous arms expenditures. In the present state of the cold war, a great deal of money is thus issued for the production of items that are kept off the market. So, when the tools of war, engines of destruction are being made, no food is being produced to feed the hungry.' That, Mr. Speaker, is the point we have reached with our unbalanced system favouring only a few people privileged by the economy or the system who have the avan-tage of controlling everything and of laying their hands on everything. If we want to have something, we must first eliminate the problem, that is to say this vast pact which weighs on the whole economy of the nation or of the nations.
So, I will say that it is difficult to deny the statement of Professor Galbraighth and others who claim that without an economic expansion based on arms production, there would be an economic breakdown in the United States.
Well, I support the statements of this professor. If, tomorrow, we were to cease the production of arms, a recession would settle on the country. There are means other than the production of arms and betting everything on war, mortgaging the whole Canadian economy, taking what the Canadians are entitled to have and what other countries are rightfully entitled to expect from the Canadians so as to invest all that in the making of tools and ships to wage war.
When we go to war, we sow destruction; when we sow destruction, we have no respect for the human being. The human being is the
27053-341}
Suggested External Aid Program primary factor in a world economy; whatever their race, their colour or their language, human beings are entitled to the greatest respect.
We should be able to organize our economy so as to give work to all unemployed in Canada who live at the expense of others, and all those who are in receipt of welfare payments and who do not participate in production. Those who are trained under the retraining program do not take part in production for Canadians or to assist foreigners. By giving work to all these people, in short, by putting the financial economy at the service of Canadians, at the service of production, we could assist others with our surplus products.
We could use our surplus production to help other countries to a large extent and we would be true Canadians. We would be proud to help foreigners.
But since our economy is unbalanced, uncontrolled, misdirected, we cannot do it. We must think of ourselves first; some Canadians lack clothing or wood or oil for-heating.
There is a lot to be done for Canadians and charity begins at home. Even if some foreign countries have great needs, great problems, we have ours. We are told that Canada is the second most prosperous country in the world; we enjoy affluence by borrowing money or letting debts pile up. That is our kind of prosperity.
Nobody can enjoy prosperity without getting into debt. We should realize that changes in our economy are necessary. Our economy should be balanced and we should accept the logical solutions which are proposed in this house. We should do something, that is we should become realistic and stop living in fantasy as we do now.
Realities do exist in Canada; there are physical things which can be achieved. There is a labour potential, capable of doubling Canada's production in two or three years. We could double the country's production if we were to put the financial interests at the service of the Canadian people. Instead of doing that, we restrict credit, we lower the purchasing power of the Canadian people and we put them out of work, we prevent them from producing and developing Canada.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I support this resolution in the hope that it will be passed quickly.
